title: Thread
body:
[[Processor Affinity]]

A thread is a single flow of execution inside a [[Processes|process]]. A process has at
least one; if it has several they all share the process's address space, which is the whole
point and the whole problem.

## What is shared and what is not

| Per process (shared by all its threads) | Per thread (private) |
|---|---|
| address space: code, [[Stack and Heap\|heap]], globals | the [[Stack]] |
| open files, [[File System Interface\|file descriptors]] | saved registers and program counter |
| the [[PCB]] | its own [[Process State]] |

**Threads share the heap and globals, and each gets its own stack.** That one line explains
most of the rest of this course: two threads writing the same global is the
[[Critical Section]] problem, and it cannot happen between two processes by accident
because their address spaces are separate.

## Why bother

- Cheaper than a process: creating one and [[Context Switching|switching]] between them
  costs less, because the address space does not change.
- Communication is free. Two threads share memory already; two processes need
  [[Inter-process Communication]] to get the same effect.
- On a multiprocessor, threads in one process actually run at the same time on different
  cores, which is where [[Amdahl's Law]] and [[Processor Affinity]] start to bite.

The cost is that every shared write is now a potential race, so you pay for it in
[[Synchronization]]: [[Locks]], [[Mutex Lock|mutexes]], [[Semaphores]].
